nodes.title: Swan conductor of an Artin–Schreier character
nodes.statement: Let K be a field of characteristic p > 0 complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field k (tier (F) or (P)); let u ∈ K with v_K(u) = −m, m > 0, p ∤ m. Let L = K(α) with α^p − α = u. Then L/K is cyclic of degree p and totally ramified, with Gal(L/K) ≅ F_p via σ ↦ σ(α) − α; its unique lower and upper break is m (G_m = G, G_{m+1} = 1); its different exponent is d(L/K) = (p − 1)(m + 1). For every nontrivial character ψ: Gal(L/K) → F^× (char F ≠ p), Sw(ψ) = m and a(ψ) = m + 1. Consequences: (i) if every break of V is < m then every break of V ⊗ ψ is m and Sw(V ⊗ ψ) = m·dim V (R01.3/additivity-twist-and-unramified-invariance (c)); (ii) for K = κ((t)) and P ∈ κ[t^{−1}] of degree d prime to p, the character of κ((t))[u]/(u^p − u − P) has break d; (iii) (Deligne 1974 (8.13)) for k finite, y ∈ k[[x]] of valuation d prime to p and L generated by the roots of T^p − T = y^{−1}, the character χ(σ) = σT − T has conductor d + 1, and the sheaf ℱ_j of Deligne 1974 §8 has Swan conductor d at infinity (8.12).
hypotheses: p ∤ m is necessary: if m = p·m′, u can be modified by an element g^p − g to lower −v(u), and the break is not m
char F ≠ p for the coefficient field of ψ
proofSteps: Extend v_K to L: p·v(α) = v(u) = −m because v(α) < 0, so v(α) = −m/p ∉ Z when p ∤ m; hence e(L/K) = p = [L:K], L/K is totally ramified, and it is Galois with group F_p since α + c (c ∈ F_p) are the roots.

Choose integers a, b with −m·a + p·b = 1 and put π_L = α^a π_K^b, a uniformiser; p ∤ a. For σ with σ(α) = α + c, c ∈ F_p^×: σ(π_L)/π_L − 1 = (1 + c/α)^a − 1 has valuation v_L(α^{-1}) = m, so v_L(σ(π_L) − π_L) = m + 1 and σ ∈ G_m \ G_{m+1} (LocalFieldsRamification layer 3 lower filtration).
For a cyclic extension of degree p with lower break m, φ(u) = u for u ≤ m, so the upper break is m; Sw(ψ) = m by R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor and a(ψ) = m + 1 (Serre 1961 n° 4.4 (b): t = n).
Hilbert's formula: d(L/K) = Σ_{i ≥ 0} (|G_i| − 1) = (m + 1)(p − 1); matches AlgebraicCurves layer 7 (Stichtenoth III.7.8) for function fields.
Deligne's finite-field statement: reduce to k algebraically closed (unramified invariance) and apply Serre 1961 n° 4.4 — or directly the computation above, valid for any perfect k.
acceptance: K = F_q((1/x)) at ∞, u = x^d with p ∤ d: Sw = d (Deligne (8.12))
PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology RD.6: polynomial twists L_P with deg P = d > every break of M have all breaks d

nodes.title: The conductor exponent of an elliptic curve
nodes.statement: Let K be as in R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor (perfect residue field of characteristic p, tier (F) or (P)), R = O_K, and E/K an elliptic curve given by a Weierstrass curve W over K with W.IsElliptic. For a prime ℓ ≠ p let V_ℓ E = T_ℓ E ⊗ Q_ℓ with its continuous G_K-action (R01.6/tate-module-of-an-abelian-variety, compared with EllipticCurves layer 2 by R01.6/elliptic-tate-module-comparison). Define f(E) := a(V_ℓ₀ E) with ℓ₀ the least prime different from p, ε(E) := codim (V_ℓ₀ E)^{I_K} and δ(E) := Sw(V_ℓ₀ E), so f(E) = ε(E) + δ(E). Theorem part: (i) for every prime ℓ ≠ p, a(V_ℓ E) = f(E), ε and δ are independent of ℓ, and δ(E) = Sw(E[ℓ]); (ii) ε(E) = 0, 1, 2 according as the minimal equation W.minimal R has good, multiplicative or additive reduction (Mathlib HasGoodReduction, HasMultiplicativeReduction, HasAdditiveReduction); (iii) δ(E) = 0 when p ≥ 5, and when E has good or multiplicative reduction; (iv) a(V_ℓ E^∨) = a(H¹) = f(E). For a number field F and E/F, N_E := ∏_v 𝔭_v^{f(E_{F_v})}, with exponent 0 exactly at the places of good reduction.
hypotheses: ℓ ≠ p (the residue characteristic, not the characteristic of K)
reduction types refer to the minimal equation W.minimal R, never to a bare integral equation
the canonical choice ℓ₀ makes the definition choice-free; independence of ℓ is a theorem
proofSteps: Independence of ℓ for ε: by (ii), whose proof uses Néron–Ogg–Shafarevich (EllipticCurves layer 4: good ⇔ unramified for ℓ ≠ p), the Tate curve for multiplicative reduction (dim V^{I} = 1, R01.2/weil-deligne-required-examples), and for additive reduction: potentially good — inertia acts through a nontrivial finite group of automorphisms of the reduction over a finite extension, and 1 − α is an isogeny for α ≠ 1, so V^{I} = 0; potentially multiplicative — V ≅ χ ⊗ V(Tate) with χ ramified quadratic, so V^{I} = 0.

Independence of ℓ for δ: δ(E) = Sw(E[ℓ]) for ℓ ≠ p by R01.3/reduction-does-not-increase-the-conductor (a); in the potentially good case the character of ρ(P_K) on V_ℓ is integer valued and independent of ℓ (traces of automorphisms α of the reduction: tr α = 1 + deg α − deg(1 − α), EllipticCurves layer 3), hence so is Sw; in the potentially multiplicative case δ = 2·Sw(χ) (Brumer–Kramer §6: each term is independent of ℓ; Serre 1970 §2.1 C3).

(iii): for p ≥ 5 the inertia image in the potentially good case has order dividing 24, prime to p, so P_K acts trivially; χ quadratic is tame for p odd; good and multiplicative reduction have P_K acting trivially.
(iv): V_ℓ E^∨ ≅ V_ℓ E(−1) by the Weil pairing (R01.6), and twisting by the unramified χ_ℓ does not change a (R01.3/additivity-twist-and-unramified-invariance (c)).

nodes.title: Ogg's formula: the algorithmic exponent is the ramification-theoretic conductor
nodes.statement: Let K be complete for a normalised discrete valuation with perfect residue field k of characteristic p (any p, including 2 and 3; tier (F) or (P)), R = O_K, E/K an elliptic curve, W a minimal Weierstrass equation (W.minimal R) with discriminant Δ_min, X → Spec R the minimal proper regular model of E (StableReduction layer 5) and m the number of irreducible components of the geometric special fibre X ⊗_k k̄, equivalently the component count of the ReductionSymbol produced by Tate's algorithm over the strict henselisation (EllipticCurves layer 4, with the configurations of NeronModelsAndSemistableAbelianVarieties R11.2). Then v_K(Δ_min) = f(E) + m − 1, where f(E) = a(V_ℓ E) (R01.3/conductor-of-an-elliptic-curve). Equivalently, the algorithmic (Ogg) exponent v(Δ_min) − m + 1 of EllipticCurves layer 4 equals the ramification-theoretic conductor exponent. Scope of closure: for p ≥ 5 the statement is proved here by a direct case check; for p ∈ {2, 3} it is deduced from R01.3/saito-conductor-discriminant, whose inputs carry the recorded gap 'Saito's conductor–discriminant theorem'.
hypotheses: k perfect; m counts geometric components (after passing to k̄); both sides are unchanged by passage to the completed strict henselisation
W must be minimal: v(Δ) of a nonminimal equation exceeds v(Δ_min) by a positive multiple of 12
the identity is between the algorithmic exponent and a(V_ℓ E) for ℓ ≠ p; residue characteristic 2 is not dropped
proofSteps: Reduce to k algebraically closed: v(Δ_min), f(E) (R01.3/additivity-twist-and-unramified-invariance (d)) and m are unchanged by the completed maximal unramified extension (EllipticCurves layer 4 minimal-model invariance; R11.2/minimal-regular-smooth-locus works over a strictly henselian base).

p ≥ 5 (direct): δ = 0 (R01.3/conductor-of-an-elliptic-curve (iii)), so f = ε; read v(Δ_min) and m off each ReductionSymbol (Tate's algorithm, EllipticCurves layer 4; configurations and component counts from R11.2/kodaira-geometric-configurations and the tame discriminant valuations recorded in R11.2/wild-kodaira-comparison): I_0: 0 = 0 + 1 − 1; I_n: n = 1 + n − 1; II: 2 = 2 + 1 − 1; III: 3 = 2 + 2 − 1; IV: 4 = 2 + 3 − 1; I_0*: 6 = 2 + 5 − 1; I_n*: n + 6 = 2 + (n + 5) − 1; IV*: 8 = 2 + 7 − 1; III*: 9 = 2 + 8 − 1; II*: 10 = 2 + 9 − 1.

All p (uniform): apply R01.3/saito-conductor-discriminant to the minimal regular model: −Art(X/S) = ord Δ_{X/S}, with ord Δ_{X/S} = v(Δ_min) and −Art(X/S) = f(E) + m − 1 (χ(X_K̄) = 0, χ(X_k̄) = m − 1 + ε(E), Swan term δ(E)) (Saito 1988 Cor. 2 as stated by Liu 1994 and Brumer–Kramer §6; DDT §2.2: Ogg's formula, proved by Saito for p = 2).

nodes.title: Saito's conductor–discriminant theorem for arithmetic surfaces
nodes.statement: Let R be a complete discrete valuation ring with perfect residue field k of characteristic p and fraction field K, S = Spec R, and f: X → S a proper flat morphism with X regular, generic fibre X_K a smooth geometrically connected curve of genus g ≥ 1. For ℓ ≠ p define the Artin conductor of X/S, Art(X/S) := χ(X_K̄) − χ(X_k̄) − Sw H¹(X_K̄, Q_ℓ), with χ the ℓ-adic étale Euler characteristic and Sw the Swan conductor of R01.3/breaks-and-swan-conductor; let Δ_{X/S} be Deligne's discriminant of X/S. Then −Art(X/S) = ord(Δ_{X/S}) (Saito 1988, Theorem 1). Genus-one specialisation: if X is the minimal regular model of an elliptic curve E/K, then ord(Δ_{X/S}) = v_K(Δ_min) (Saito 1988, Cor. 2), H¹(X_K̄, Q_ℓ) = (V_ℓ E)^∨, χ(X_K̄) = 0 and χ(X_k̄) = m − 1 + ε(E), so −Art(X/S) = f(E) + m − 1 — Ogg's formula.
hypotheses: regularity of X is essential; Art(X/S) ≤ 0 with equality iff X → S is smooth (or g = 1 and the reduced special fibre is smooth)
the étale cohomology of the fibres, the specialisation identity b_1(X_k̄) = dim H¹(X_K̄)^{I_K} and Deligne's discriminant have no owner in the atlas: recorded gap
proofSteps: Saito's proof (not read here; Duke Math. J. 57 (1988) is not freely available): compare Deligne's discriminant, defined through the Mumford isomorphism det Rf_*(ω^{⊗2}) ≅ (det Rf_*ω)^{⊗13} ⊗ (discriminant), with the localised Chern class of the singular locus, and identify the latter with −Art(X/S) through Bloch's conductor formula in relative dimension one; uniform in p.

Genus one: Deligne's discriminant of the minimal regular model is the minimal Weierstrass discriminant; the special fibre of the minimal regular model has b_0 = 1, b_2 = m and b_1 = dim V^{I_K} = 2 − ε(E) (Néron model identity component, R11.2/minimal-regular-smooth-locus), giving χ(X_k̄) = m − 1 + ε.

Statement as read: Liu 1994 recalls Art(X/S) and ord Δ = −Art(X/S) ([Sa1] Theorem 1) and Ogg's formula ([Sa1] Cor. 2); Brumer–Kramer §6 and DDT §2.2 attribute the residue-characteristic-2 case of Ogg's formula to Saito.

nodes.title: Values and bounds of elliptic conductor exponents; isogeny invariance
nodes.statement: Let K be a nonarchimedean local field of residue characteristic p (tier (F)) and E/K an elliptic curve. (a) f(E) = 0 for good, 1 for multiplicative and 2 + δ(E) for additive reduction, with δ(E) = 0 if p ≥ 5. (b) If E has additive potentially multiplicative reduction, E is the quadratic twist by a ramified character χ of a curve with multiplicative reduction and f(E) = 2·a(χ) = 2 + 2·Sw(χ); over Q_2 this gives f ∈ {4, 6}. (c) Bounds (Lockhart–Rosen–Silverman; Brumer–Kramer Theorem 6.2 for g = 1): f(E) ≤ 2 + 3·v_K(3) + 6·v_K(2); in particular for K = Q_p: f_2 ≤ 8, f_3 ≤ 5 and f_p ≤ 2 for p ≥ 5, and the bounds 8 and 5 are attained (curves of conductor 2^8 and 3^5 exist). (d) Isogeny invariance: if E and E′ are isogenous over K, f(E) = f(E′); over a number field N_E = N_{E′}. (e) Global over Q: p | N_E iff E has bad reduction at p (for every p, including 2 and 3); v_p(N_E) = 1 iff E has multiplicative reduction at p; N_E divides 2^8·3^5·∏_{p ≥ 5, p | N_E} p².
hypotheses: mixed characteristic for the bound in (c) as stated (v_K(2), v_K(3) are absolute ramification data); finite residue field
proofSteps: (a) is R01.3/conductor-of-an-elliptic-curve (ii)–(iii).

(b): potentially multiplicative reduction gives V_ℓ E ≅ χ ⊗ V_ℓ(E_q) (Tate curve, EllipticCurves layer 4); V^{I} = 0 and Sw(V) = 2·Sw(χ) (R01.3/additivity-twist-and-unramified-invariance), and Sw(χ) ∈ {1, 2} over Q_2 by R01.3/tame-conductor-computations (e).

(c): Brumer–Kramer Theorem 6.2 (read on the page image, printed p. 243): for an abelian variety of dimension g over a p-adic field K, f(A/K) ≤ 2g + e_K[p·d + (p − 1)·λ_p(d)] with d = ⌊2g/(p − 1)⌋ and λ_p(d) = Σ i·r_i·p^i for d = Σ r_i p^i; for g = 1 this is 2 + 6e_K at p = 2 (d = 2, λ_2(2) = 2) and 2 + 3e_K at p = 3 (d = 1, λ_3(1) = 0), and 2 for p ≥ 5 (d = 0). Their proof: δ(E) = Sw(E[ℓ]) for an auxiliary ℓ ≠ p; for ℓ = 3 at p = 2 the image of P_K lies in SL_2(F_3) (the determinant is the mod-3 cyclotomic character, unramified at 2), whose 2-Sylow subgroups have order 8, and for ℓ = 2 at p = 3 in GL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3 with 3-Sylow of order 3; Hensel's bound on the different d ≤ e − 1 + v_L(e) (LocalFieldsRamification layer 3) bounds Σ_{i≥1}(|G_i| − 1) and hence Sw (Serre 1987 §4.9, (4.9.3)–(4.9.7); Brumer–Kramer Theorem 6.2); the refinement from 9 to 8 at p = 2 is Serre's 'analyse plus détaillée' and Brumer–Kramer Lemma 6.8.
(d): an isogeny induces an isomorphism V_ℓ E ≅ V_ℓ E′ of G_K-representations (R01.6/functoriality-products-and-isogenies).
(e): from (a)–(c) and N_E = ∏ p^{f_p}.
acceptance: Q_3: exponent 5 is attained (Serre 1987 §4.9 (a)); Q_2: exponent 8 is attained (§4.9 (b)); Brumer–Kramer Lemma 6.8: y² = x³ + π_M x over a 2-adic field M has f = 2 + 6e_M
y² = x³ − x over Q_2: f_2 = 5 ≤ 8
Bennett–Siksek, Lemma 3.3: for their Frey–Hellegouarch curves the level divides 2^8·(odd squarefree), using f_2 ≤ 8

nodes.title: Residual elliptic conductors away from ℓ
nodes.statement: Let K be a nonarchimedean local field of residue characteristic p, E/K an elliptic curve and ℓ ≠ p a prime; E[ℓ] is the residual representation of V_ℓ E for the lattice T_ℓ E (R01.6/torsion-and-residual-representation). Then Sw(E[ℓ]) = δ(E) and a(E[ℓ]) ≤ f(E), and: (a) if E has good reduction, a(E[ℓ]) = 0; (b) if E has multiplicative reduction, a(E[ℓ]) = 0 when ℓ | v_K(Δ_min) and = 1 otherwise; (c) if E has additive potentially multiplicative reduction and ℓ is odd, a(E[ℓ]) = f(E); (d) if E has additive potentially good reduction and ℓ does not divide the order of ρ_{E,ℓ}(I_K) (always when ℓ ≥ 5, the order having only the prime factors 2 and 3), a(E[ℓ]) = f(E). Hence for ℓ ≥ 5: a(E[ℓ]) = f(E) unless E has multiplicative reduction with ℓ | v_K(Δ_min), in which case a(E[ℓ]) = 0. Global (E/Q, ℓ ≥ 5): N(ρ̄_{E,ℓ}) = N_E^{(ℓ)} / ∏_{q ∥ N_E, q ≠ ℓ, ℓ | v_q(Δ_min)} q, where N_E^{(ℓ)} is the prime-to-ℓ part of N_E; in particular N(ρ̄_{E,ℓ}) | N_E.
hypotheses: q ≠ ℓ; the ℓ-part of a level such as Bennett–Siksek's M_0 is a weight/finite-flatness matter (AlgebraicModularFormsAndSerreWeights), not a conductor
ℓ ≥ 5 in the clean global form; for ℓ = 3 at q = 2 and ℓ = 2 at q = 3 additive potentially good reduction can lose further inertia invariants
proofSteps: Sw and the inequality: R01.3/reduction-does-not-increase-the-conductor (a), (b).

(b): split multiplicative case through the Tate curve (EllipticCurves layer 4): E[ℓ] is an extension of Z/ℓ by μ_ℓ with class the Kummer class of q, unramified iff ℓ | v(q) = v(Δ_min); the nonsplit case after the unramified quadratic twist (R01.3/additivity-twist-and-unramified-invariance (c), (d)); Serre 1987 (4.1.12) and Lemme 5.
(c): E[ℓ]|_{I_K} ≅ χ ⊗ (unipotent), χ ramified quadratic; an inertia element with χ = −1 acts as −u with u unipotent, which has no fixed vectors for ℓ odd, so E[ℓ]^{I_K} = 0 = V^{I_K}.

(d): ρ(I_K) finite of order prime to ℓ: equality in R01.3/reduction-does-not-increase-the-conductor (b); the inertia group acts on the good reduction over a finite extension through automorphisms of an elliptic curve, a group of order dividing 24.
Global: apply at each q ≠ ℓ.
acceptance: EllipticModularityEffectiveComparisons EC.3/deletion-conductor-away: the prime-to-ℓ deletion level equals N(E[ℓ])
Bennett–Siksek (3): M_0 = M/∏_{q ∥ M, ℓ | ord_q Δ} q

nodes.title: Complex conjugations and odd rank-two representations
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, F̄ an algebraic closure and G_F = Field.absoluteGaloisGroup F with its Krull topology. (1) Complex conjugations. For a real infinite place v of F (NumberField.InfinitePlace.IsReal) and a field embedding ι : F̄ → ℂ whose restriction to F is a real embedding inducing v, the image ι(F̄) is stable under complex conjugation conj = Complex.conjAe, and c_ι := ι⁻¹ ∘ conj ∘ ι ∈ G_F. Then c_ι² = 1, c_ι ≠ 1, and for two such embeddings ι, ι′ above the same v the elements c_ι, c_ι′ are conjugate in G_F; write c_v for this conjugacy class. (2) Totally odd characters. A continuous character μ : G_F → A^× with values in a topological commutative ring A is totally odd if μ(c_v) = −1 for every real place v of F (the condition does not depend on the choice of c_v in its class). (3) Odd representations. Let A be a topological commutative ring and ρ ∈ ContinuousRep G_F A M with M finite projective of rank 2 over A (R01.1/continuous-representation). ρ is odd at the real place v if det_A ρ(c_v) = −1 in A, and odd (totally odd) if it is odd at every real place of F, i.e. if det ρ is totally odd. For F = ℚ there is exactly one real place and c is any complex conjugation. When F has no real place every ρ is odd. Pinned conventions: (a) oddness depends only on the character det ρ; (b) if A is a field of characteristic ≠ 2, ρ is odd at v iff Tr ρ(c_v) = 0 iff ρ(c_v) is conjugate to diag(1, −1); (c) if 2 = 0 in A (for instance A = k a finite field of characteristic 2) then det ρ(c_v) = ±1 = 1 = −1 and every rank-two ρ is odd; the condition ‘ρ(c_v) ≠ 1’ used in characteristic two is a separate condition, named non-trivial at v, and is never part of oddness.
hypotheses: F is a number field; G_F carries the Krull topology
A is a topological commutative ring and M a finite projective A-module of rank 2 (free of rank 2 in framed coordinates)
c_v is well defined only up to conjugacy in G_F; every statement is conjugation invariant
in characteristic two oddness is automatic; ρ(c) ≠ 1 is a separate hypothesis
proofSteps: Since ι|_F lands in ℝ, conj fixes ι(F) and preserves the algebraic closure ι(F̄) of ι(F) in ℂ, so c_ι is an F-automorphism of F̄; c_ι² = 1 because conj² = 1, and c_ι ≠ 1 because F̄ is not contained in ℝ (it contains √−1).
Two embeddings above v differ by an element g ∈ G_F (ι′ = ι ∘ g after composing with conj if necessary, using that the real embedding is fixed by conj), so c_ι′ = g⁻¹ c_ι g.
det ρ is a continuous character G_F → A^× (determinant of a finite projective module of rank 2), so det ρ(c_v) is well defined on the class c_v; oddness of ρ is total oddness of det ρ.

If A is a field with char A ≠ 2, ρ(c_v)² = 1 forces ρ(c_v) to be diagonalisable with eigenvalues in {±1}; the determinant is −1 exactly when the eigenvalues are 1 and −1, exactly when the trace is 0 (traces of ±1 are ±2 ≠ 0).
Serre 1987, 1.3 fixes the convention det ρ(c) = −1 for G_ℚ; Khare–Wintenberger I §1 define S-type with ‘det ρ̄(c) = −1 for c a complex conjugation’.
acceptance: For p odd and χ̄_p : G_ℚ → F_p^× the mod-p cyclotomic character, χ̄_p ⊕ 1 is odd since c acts on μ_p by inversion; any ρ̄ with det ρ̄ = χ̄_p is odd (the case of E[p], R01.6/determinant-and-oddness).
Over F_5, ρ = χ_{−3} ⊕ χ_{−4} (quadratic characters of ℚ(√−3), ℚ(i)) has ρ(c) = −1 ≠ 1 but det ρ(c) = 1, so it is not odd: ‘ρ(c) ≠ 1’ is not oddness.

In characteristic two the trivial representation of G_ℚ on F_2² is odd but not non-trivial at c; the representation of G_ℚ on E[2] for E : y² = x³ − 2 is odd and non-trivial at c (c is a transposition of the three roots of x³ − 2).

nodes.title: Odd irreducible residual representations are absolutely irreducible (odd p), and the characteristic-two case
nodes.statement: (a) Rationality lemma. Let k be a field, Γ a group and ρ : Γ → GL_2(k). Suppose ρ(Γ) contains a non-scalar element g whose characteristic polynomial splits over k. Then every ρ(Γ)-stable line of k′² (k′/k any field extension) is k-rational; hence ρ is irreducible iff ρ ⊗_k k′ is irreducible, and ρ is irreducible iff it is absolutely irreducible (R01.1/absolutely-irreducible). (b) Odd p. Let F be a number field with a real place v, k a field of characteristic ≠ 2 (for example a finite field of odd characteristic p), and ρ̄ : G_F → GL_2(k) continuous and odd at v. If ρ̄ is irreducible over k then it is absolutely irreducible. In particular for p odd an odd ρ̄ : G_ℚ → GL_2(F_p) irreducible over F_p is absolutely irreducible. (c) Characteristic two. Let k have characteristic 2 and ρ̄ : G_F → GL_2(k) continuous. If ρ̄(c_v) ≠ 1 for some real place v, irreducible implies absolutely irreducible (ρ̄(c_v) is a transvection with a unique, k-rational, invariant line). Without that hypothesis the implication fails: for a cyclic cubic field L/ℚ (for instance the real subfield of ℚ(ζ_7)) and a generator σ of Gal(L/ℚ), the representation G_ℚ → Gal(L/ℚ) → GL_2(F_2), σ ↦ [[0, 1], [1, 1]] (companion matrix of x² + x + 1), is odd (characteristic 2), has image of order 3, is irreducible over F_2 and becomes reducible over F_4 = F_2(ω), where it is ω^a ⊕ ω^{2a}.
hypotheses: (a) needs only one non-scalar element with split characteristic polynomial; no finiteness or continuity
(b) needs char k ≠ 2: then ρ̄(c_v) has the distinct eigenvalues 1 and −1 in k
(c) needs ρ̄(c_v) ≠ 1; oddness itself carries no information in characteristic 2
proofSteps: (a) If g is non-scalar with split characteristic polynomial, either g has two distinct eigenvalues in k (exactly two invariant lines over k′, both k-rational) or one eigenvalue λ ∈ k with g − λ nilpotent of rank 1 (exactly one invariant line ker(g − λ), k-rational). A ρ(Γ)-stable line of k′² is g-stable, hence one of these, hence k-rational and already ρ(Γ)-stable over k.

(b) det ρ̄(c_v) = −1 and ρ̄(c_v)² = 1 give eigenvalues 1 and −1, distinct since char k ≠ 2, so g = ρ̄(c_v) satisfies (a). This is Serre 1987, 3.3 (b′); Serre's sentence treats only a decomposition over F̄_p into a direct sum of two lines, while (a) also covers a reducible but indecomposable ρ̄ ⊗ F̄_p (its unique stable line is ρ̄(c)-stable, hence an eigenline of ρ̄(c), hence F_p-rational); see sourceIssues.

(c) In characteristic 2, ρ̄(c_v)² = 1 and ρ̄(c_v) ≠ 1 force ρ̄(c_v) = 1 + n with n² = 0, n ≠ 0, a transvection; (a) applies. In the counterexample the image is generated by an element of order 3 with irreducible characteristic polynomial x² + x + 1 over F_2; over F_4 its eigenlines are stable, and complex conjugation acts trivially because L is totally real.
The reduction of finite images: a continuous ρ̄ with discrete finite coefficients has finite image (R01.1/finite-coefficients-and-finite-quotients), so ρ̄(c_v) is a genuine element of a finite group.
acceptance: Instance (Serre 1987, 3.3): for p odd, ρ : G_ℚ → GL_2(F_p) with det ρ = χ̄_p (the mod-p cyclotomic character) is odd, so irreducible over F_p implies absolutely irreducible; this is the input of EllipticCurveModularity:R29.1 for E[p].
Non-example in characteristic 2 (statement (c)): the cyclic-cubic representation over F_2 with image of order 3 is odd, irreducible over F_2 and not absolutely irreducible.
Positive characteristic-two instance: E[2] for E : y² = x³ − 2 has image GL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3 with ρ̄(c) a transvection; it is irreducible and absolutely irreducible.

Oddness is needed in odd characteristic too: over F_5 the cyclic-cubic representation σ ↦ [[0, −1], [1, −1]] (characteristic polynomial x² + x + 1, irreducible over F_5) has image of order 3, is irreducible over F_5, splits over F_25, and is even (ρ̄(c) = 1).

nodes.title: Dickson's classification of finite subgroups of PGL_2(F̄_p), with the coefficient field visible, its consequences and the p = 2 refinement
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, k̄ an algebraic closure of F_p (discrete), π : GL_2(k̄) → PGL_2(k̄) = Matrix.ProjGenLinGroup (Fin 2) k̄ the projection, and F_q ⊂ k̄ the subfield with q elements. (a) [Dickson] Every finite subgroup H ⊂ PGL_2(k̄) satisfies one of: (i) H fixes a point of P¹(k̄), i.e. is conjugate into the image of the upper-triangular Borel; (ii) H is conjugate to PSL_2(F_q) or PGL_2(F_q) for some power q of p; (iii) H is isomorphic to A_4, S_4, A_5, or to the dihedral group of order 2n (Mathlib DihedralGroup n) for some n ≥ 2 with p ∤ n. For q ≥ 4 all subgroups of PGL_2(k̄) isomorphic to PSL_2(F_q) are conjugate, and likewise for PGL_2(F_q). Elements of A_4, S_4, A_5 have order 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5; PSL_2(F_q) is simple for q ≥ 4. (b) [GL_2 form, coefficient field visible] Let k ⊂ k̄ be a finite field and G ⊂ GL_2(k) a subgroup acting absolutely irreducibly on k̄². Then π(G) is not cyclic and fixes no point of P¹(k̄), and either π(G) is dihedral of order 2n (n ≥ 2, p ∤ n), or π(G) ≅ A_4, S_4 or A_5, or π(G) is conjugate in PGL_2(k̄) to PSL_2(F_0) or PGL_2(F_0) where F_0 ⊂ k is the subfield generated by the values Tr(g)²/det(g), g ∈ G. (c) [linear form] If π(G) is conjugate to PSL_2(F_0) or PGL_2(F_0) with |F_0| ≥ 4, then after conjugation in GL_2(k̄) the commutator subgroup [G, G] equals SL_2(F_0) and G ⊂ k̄^× · GL_2(F_0); the abelianisation of π(G) has order 1 (PSL_2) or gcd(2, |F_0| − 1) (PGL_2). Conversely if G ⊃ SL_2(F_1) for a subfield F_1 with |F_1| ≥ 4, then π(G) is conjugate to PSL_2(F_0) or PGL_2(F_0) for a field F_0 ⊃ F_1; in particular for p ≥ 5 and G ⊃ SL_2(F_p) the projective image is PSL_2(F_{p^s}) or PGL_2(F_{p^s}) and its abelianisation has order ≤ 2. (d) [p = 2, Khare–Wintenberger I Lemma 6.1] If p = 2 and G ⊂ GL_2(F̄_2) is finite, irreducible and solvable, then π(G) is dihedral of order 2n with n odd ≥ 3 (S_4 does not occur; A_4 occurs only as the Borel subgroup of PGL_2(F_4) and is reducible). If G is irreducible and not solvable, π(G) is conjugate to PGL_2(F_0) = PSL_2(F_0) ≅ SL_2(F_0) with |F_0| = 2^r, r ≥ 2. (e) [order criteria] If G is irreducible and π(G) contains an element of order > 5, then π(G) is not exceptional; if moreover G is solvable, π(G) is dihedral; if G is irreducible, π(G) contains an element of order > 5 and π(G) normalises no Cartan (equivalently G is not contained in the normaliser of a torus), then G contains a conjugate of SL_2(F_p) (Clozel–Thorne Lemma 7.5).
hypotheses: k̄ = F̄_p with the discrete topology; all groups finite
(b)–(e) concern subgroups of GL_2 over finite fields of characteristic p; absolute irreducibility means irreducibility on k̄²
the simplicity of PSL_2(F_0) and perfectness of SL_2(F_0) need |F_0| ≥ 4
(a) is Dickson's theorem, quoted from Dickson 1901 §§255–260 through Darmon–Diamond–Taylor Theorem 2.47(b); its proof is sketched, not decomposed
proofSteps: (a) Dickson 1901 §260 lists the subgroups of LF(2, s) = PSL_2(F_s) and §261 proves simplicity for s > 3; DDT Theorem 2.47(b) states the PGL_2(F̄_ℓ) form used by the consumers. Sketch: a finite H lies in PGL_2(F_s) ⊂ PSL_2(F_{s²}). If p ∤ |H|, lift H to characteristic 0 (Serre 1972 Prop. 16, method 2) and use the finite subgroups of SO_3(ℝ): cyclic, dihedral, A_4, S_4, A_5. If p | |H|, the p-elements are unipotent with unique fixed points (R01.4/p-subgroups-and-borel-subgroups); one Sylow p-subgroup gives (i), two with distinct fixed points generate PSL_2 of the field generated by the products of their parameters (Serre 1972 Prop. 15 over F_p, Dickson §§249–255 in general), and its normaliser is PGL_2 of that field.

(b) A cyclic π(G) makes G abelian (a central extension of a cyclic group), so G has a common eigenvector over k̄ (tauceti:TauCeti.exists_unitHom_jointEigenvector_of_pairwise_commute_of_isAlgClosed), contradicting absolute irreducibility; a fixed point of π(G) is a G-stable line. The function g ↦ Tr(g)²/det(g) is a class function on PGL_2, so its values on π(G) ⊂ PGL_2(k) lie in k; on PSL_2(F_0) it takes every square of F_0 (companion matrices), and the squares of F_0 generate F_0, so F_0 ⊂ k.

(c) Scalars are central, so [λA, μB] = [A, B] and [G, G] ⊂ [GL_2(F_0), GL_2(F_0)] = SL_2(F_0); [G, G] maps onto [π(G), π(G)] ⊇ PSL_2(F_0) (perfect, mathlib:SL2Simple.PSL_commutator_eq_top), so [G,G]·{±1} = SL_2(F_0), and perfectness of SL_2(F_0) (mathlib:Matrix.SL2.commutator_eq_top) gives [G,G] = SL_2(F_0). Conversely PSL_2(F_1) ⊂ π(G) is non-solvable (mathlib:Group.IsPerfect.not_isSolvable), so π(G) is not Borel, dihedral, A_4, S_4; if π(G) ≅ A_5 then π(G) = PSL_2(F_1) with |F_1| ∈ {4, 5}; otherwise (a)(ii), and F_0 ⊃ F_1 by the trace-field argument of (b). PGL_2(F_0)^{ab} = F_0^×/F_0^{×2} via det.

(d) As in Khare–Wintenberger I Lemma 6.1: a 2-element of GL_2(F̄_2) is unipotent of order ≤ 2, so S_4 (elements of order 4) is excluded; the normal Klein subgroup of A_4 lies in a unipotent Sylow 2-subgroup (R01.4/p-subgroups-and-borel-subgroups), whose unique fixed line is G-stable. Dihedral of even n contains a central involution, i.e. a normal 2-subgroup, again fixing a line; so n is odd. Non-solvable: (a) leaves PSL_2(F_0) = PGL_2(F_0) (char 2) with |F_0| ≥ 4; PGL_2(F̄_2) ≅ SL_2(F̄_2) via mathlib:Matrix.ProjectiveSpecialLinearGroup.isoPSLOfAlgClosed and SL_2 = PSL_2 in characteristic 2.

(e) A_4, S_4, A_5 have no element of order > 5 (Serre 1972 Prop. 16); solvable irreducible images not exceptional are dihedral by (a); in the last case (a) leaves PSL_2/PGL_2(F_{p^a}) and (c) gives SL_2(F_{p^a}) ⊃ SL_2(F_p).
acceptance: Check the exclusion of A_4 in characteristic 2 by exhibiting the normal Klein subgroup inside the unipotent radical of the Borel of SL_2(F_4) ≅ A_5, and check that over F̄_3 the irreducible group SL_2(F_3) has projective image PSL_2(F_3) ≅ A_4, so the dyadic refinement is genuinely characteristic 2.

Projective images in practice: S_3 ≅ GL_2(F_2) = PGL_2(F_2) (dihedral of order 6, from E[2] of y² = x³ − 2); A_4 ≅ PSL_2(F_3) and S_4 ≅ PGL_2(F_3) (from SL_2(F_3) ⊂ GL_2(F_3) = image of E[3] for a non-CM E with surjective mod-3 image); A_5 ≅ PSL_2(F_5) ≅ SL_2(F_4) (from SL_2(F_5) ⊂ GL_2(F_5)).
A_5 ⊂ PGL_2(F_p) for p ≠ 2, 5 occurs only for p ≡ ±1 mod 5 (Serre 1972 2.6(iii)); for p = 7 the projective image of a subgroup of GL_2(F_7) is never A_5.

nodes.title: Subgroups of GL_2(F_ℓ): Serre's Propositions 15–18
nodes.statement: Let ℓ be a prime, V a two-dimensional F_ℓ-vector space and G ⊂ GL(V) ≅ GL_2(F_ℓ) a subgroup. (a) [Serre 1972 Prop. 15] If ℓ divides |G| then G contains SL(V) or G is contained in a Borel subgroup. (b) [Prop. 16 and 2.6] If ℓ ∤ |G|, let H = π(G) ⊂ PGL(V). Then H is cyclic and G lies in a Cartan subgroup, or H is dihedral and G lies in the normaliser of a Cartan subgroup (and not in the Cartan subgroup when H is non-cyclic), or H ≅ A_4, S_4 or A_5, the last only if ℓ ≡ ±1 mod 5; for ℓ = 2, 3 only the first two occur. Every finite subgroup of PGL_2(K) of order prime to char K, K any field, is cyclic, dihedral, A_4, S_4 or A_5. (c) Hence (the form used by Deligne–Serre 7.2): if G acts semisimply on V, then G contains SL(V), or lies in a Cartan subgroup, or lies in the normaliser of a Cartan subgroup but not in it, or π(G) ≅ A_4, S_4, A_5; the reducible semisimple case is the split-Cartan case. (d) [Prop. 17] If G contains a Cartan subgroup C (resp. a split half-Cartan C′) and ℓ ≠ 5 when C is split, then G = GL(V), or G lies in a Borel subgroup, or G lies in the normaliser of a Cartan subgroup. (e) [Prop. 18] If ℓ ≠ 2, G contains a Cartan subgroup or a split half-Cartan, and G is normal in GL(V), then G = GL(V).
hypotheses: ℓ prime and G ⊂ GL_2(F_ℓ) (the prime field); Cartan subgroups as in R01.4/cartan-subgroups-and-normalisers
(d) excludes ℓ = 5 for split C (Serre's remark: S_4 occurs); (e) excludes ℓ = 2
proofSteps: (a) Serre's proof: an element of order ℓ is a transvection fixing a unique line; if all these lines coincide, G stabilises it (Borel); otherwise G contains [[1, a], [0, 1]] and [[1, 0], [b, 1]] with ab ≠ 0, and these generate SL_2(F_ℓ) (Bourbaki A III p. 104 prop. 17, or the transvection generation mathlib:Matrix.SL2.transvection_induction).

(b) Prop. 16 for K = F_ℓ: by lifting to characteristic 0 and the finite rotation groups; a cyclic H lies in a unique Cartan of PGL(V) when nontrivial; a dihedral H normalises the Cartan containing its index-2 cyclic subgroup; A_5 needs elements of order 5 in PGL_2(F_ℓ), i.e. 5 | ℓ(ℓ² − 1).
(c) combines (a) and (b): a semisimple G with ℓ | |G| cannot lie in a Borel unless reducible-semisimple, which forces ℓ ∤ |G|; so ℓ | |G| gives SL(V) ⊂ G.
(d) If ℓ | |G| use (a) and det(C) = F_ℓ^×; otherwise C has image of order ℓ ± 1 ≥ 6 in PGL(V) and A_4, S_4, A_5 have no element of order ≥ 6.
(e) Normal subgroups of GL_2(F_ℓ), ℓ ≥ 5, are central or contain SL_2 (R01.4/normal-subgroups-and-automorphisms-of-psl2-pgl2); ℓ = 3 by PGL_2(F_3) ≅ S_4.
acceptance: Instance: the image of the mod-ℓ representation of a non-CM elliptic curve with a rational ℓ-isogeny lies in a Borel subgroup; the mod-ℓ image of a CM curve over ℚ with ℓ inert in the CM field is the normaliser of a non-split Cartan, case (b)/(c).
Serre's remark after Prop. 17: for ℓ = 5 and split C, π(G) ≅ S_4 occurs, so the hypothesis ℓ ≠ 5 cannot be dropped.
For ℓ = 3: GL_2(F_3) has PGL_2(F_3) ≅ S_4 and the subgroup SL_2(F_3) of order 24 is not in a Borel and contains SL(V), consistent with (a).

nodes.title: Cartan subgroups of GL_2 over a finite field and their normalisers
nodes.statement: Let k be a finite field with q elements, V a two-dimensional k-vector space and GL(V) ≅ GL_2(k). (1) Split Cartan: for two distinct lines D_1 ≠ D_2 of V, C_s(D_1, D_2) := {s ∈ GL(V) : sD_1 = D_1, sD_2 = D_2} ≅ (k^×)², the diagonal torus in a basis adapted to D_1 ⊕ D_2. (2) Non-split Cartan: for a subalgebra k′ ⊂ End_k(V) which is a field with q² elements, C_ns(k′) := k′^× ⊂ GL(V), cyclic of order q² − 1; in coordinates it is TauCeti.GL2NonSplitTorus k k′ (left multiplication on k′ ≅ k² in a chosen basis); for q odd and ε ∈ k^× a non-square it is conjugate to {[[a, εb], [b, a]] : (a, b) ≠ (0, 0)}. (3) Normalisers: N(C) := normaliser of C in GL(V). For a split Cartan, N(C) is the stabiliser of the pair {D_1, D_2}; for a non-split Cartan, N(C) is the group of k′-semilinear automorphisms s(ax) = a^q s(x). If C is non-split, or split with q ≥ 3, then [N(C) : C] = 2, every element of N(C) ∖ C has trace 0 and square scalar, and the images C̄ ⊂ N̄ in PGL(V) are cyclic of order q ∓ 1 (− split, + non-split) and dihedral of order 2(q ∓ 1). (4) Borel: B(D) := stabiliser of a line D, of order q(q − 1)², TauCeti.GL2Borel k for D = ⟨e_1⟩. Half-Cartan (Serre): the subgroup of C_s(D_1, D_2) acting trivially on D_2.
hypotheses: k finite with q = |k| elements; q ≥ 3 for statements about split normalisers (for q = 2 the split Cartan is trivial)
Cartan subgroups are defined basis-free; matrix models are API
over F̄_p (consumers using algebraically closed coefficients) the image of a finite subgroup of a Cartan of GL_2(k) is diagonalisable over k̄
proofSteps: k′ = k[C] is a commutative semisimple k-algebra of rank 2 with C = k′^× (split: k × k; non-split: F_{q²}); an element of N(C) induces a k-algebra automorphism of k′, trivial exactly on C, and Aut_k(k′) has order 2 (swap, resp. Frobenius), so [N(C) : C] = 2 (Serre 1972 §2.2).

For s ∈ N(C) ∖ C, s² ∈ C commutes with s and is fixed by the swap/Frobenius, so s² ∈ k^× (scalar) and the characteristic polynomial is X² − s², trace 0 (split: s is antidiagonal; non-split: s(x) = λ x^q, s² = N(λ)).

The union of the Cartan subgroups is the set of semisimple (order prime to p) elements; for p ≠ 2 an element with Tr² − 4 det ≠ 0 lies in exactly one Cartan, split iff Tr² − 4det is a square (Serre 1972 §2.1).

Tau Ceti provides the non-split torus with its order q² − 1, its index, its non-conjugacy into the Borel, and the conjugacy classification of non-scalar elements by trace and determinant; the diagonal torus and its Weyl element normaliser are TauCeti.diagGL and TauCeti.gl2WeylElement_mem_normalizer_diagonalTorus.
acceptance: |C_s| = (q − 1)², |C_ns| = q² − 1, |N(C_s)| = 2(q − 1)², |N(C_ns)| = 2(q² − 1); for q = 3, N(C_s) is dihedral of order 8 and N(C_ns) is the semidihedral Sylow 2-subgroup of GL_2(F_3) of order 16.

CM instance: for E/ℚ with CM by an order in K and ℓ ∤ disc(K) inert in K, the image of G_ℚ on E[ℓ] is the normaliser of the non-split Cartan (O_K/ℓ)^× and the image of G_K is the Cartan itself; for ℓ split in K it is N(C_s).

nodes.title: p-subgroups of GL_2 in characteristic p fix a unique line
nodes.statement: Let k be a field of characteristic p > 0 (finite or algebraically closed) and P ⊂ GL_2(k) a nontrivial finite p-subgroup. Then every element of P is unipotent, P is elementary abelian of exponent p, conjugate into the upper unitriangular group {[[1, b], [0, 1]]} ≅ (k, +), and P fixes exactly one line D = V^P of k̄² (which is k-rational); the normaliser of P in GL_2(k) lies in the Borel subgroup B(D). Consequently: (i) a subgroup G ⊂ GL_2(k) with a nontrivial normal p-subgroup is reducible, with G-stable line V^{O_p(G)}; (ii) the Sylow p-subgroups of GL_2(F_q) are the unipotent radicals of the q + 1 Borel subgroups, of order q; (iii) for G ⊂ GL_2(k) reducible over k̄ with p | |G|, the Sylow p-subgroup of G is normal and fixes the unique G-stable line; (iv) a finite subgroup of PGL_2(k̄) with a nontrivial normal p-subgroup fixes a point of P¹(k̄).
hypotheses: char k = p > 0
P finite (for k finite automatic)
proofSteps: An element u of p-power order satisfies (u − 1)^{p^a} = u^{p^a} − 1 = 0, so u is unipotent; in dimension 2, (u − 1)² = 0, hence u^p = 1.

For u ≠ 1 unipotent, ker(u − 1) is the unique u-invariant line. A nontrivial p-group fixes a nonzero vector of k̄² (orbit counting on the finite F_p-span, or mathlib:IsPGroup.card_modEq_card_fixedPoints on the line set over a finite field); all its non-identity elements then share that line, so P is upper unitriangular in an adapted basis, isomorphic to a subgroup of (k, +).
If g normalises P then g permutes the P-fixed lines, of which there is one; so g ∈ B(D). (i) and (iv) follow since O_p(G) is characteristic in G (Mathlib IsPGroup, Sylow).
(ii) |GL_2(F_q)| = q(q − 1)²(q + 1) and the unipotent radical of the Borel has order q (tauceti:TauCeti.GL2Borel.card_eq).
acceptance: For q = 4: the Sylow 2-subgroups of SL_2(F_4) ≅ A_5 are the five Klein four-groups, the unipotent radicals of the five Borels; this is the exclusion of A_4 in characteristic 2.
Over F_3 the group SL_2(F_3) has Sylow 3-subgroups of order 3 that are not normal (four of them), so SL_2(F_3) is irreducible; consistent with (iii).

For a finite Galois extension E/ℚ_p with wild inertia P ≠ 1 embedded in GL_2(F) (char F = p), the image of the decomposition group lies in a Borel and P maps into its unipotent radical (SmallRamificationAndAbelianVarietyBaseCases:R25.1/wild-image-borel-normal-form).

nodes.title: Dihedral projective image if and only if induced from an index-two subgroup
nodes.statement: Let Γ be a profinite group, k an algebraically closed field (any characteristic) and ρ : Γ → GL_2(k) a homomorphism whose projectivisation π∘ρ has open kernel and finite image (automatic for k = F̄_p discrete and ρ continuous). (a) The following are equivalent: (1) ρ is irreducible and π(ρ(Γ)) is dihedral of order 2n for some n ≥ 2; (2) ρ ≅ Ind_Δ^Γ χ (R01.1/continuous-induction) for an open subgroup Δ of index 2 and a continuous character χ : Δ → k^× with χ ≠ χ^σ, where χ^σ(δ) = χ(σ δ σ⁻¹) for any σ ∈ Γ ∖ Δ. (b) In (2), ρ|_Δ ≅ χ ⊕ χ^σ, π(ρ(Δ)) is cyclic of order n = order of χ/χ^σ (so char k ∤ n), elements of ρ(Γ ∖ Δ) have trace 0, and det ρ = (χ|_{Ver}) · ε_Δ (R01.1/determinant-of-induced-representation, ε_Δ the quadratic character with kernel Δ). For n ≥ 3, Δ is unique: it is the preimage of the cyclic subgroup of order n; for n = 2 (Klein image) there are exactly three such Δ. (c) If char k ≠ 2 and ρ is irreducible, ρ ≅ Ind_Δ^Γ χ for some χ iff ρ ⊗ ε_Δ ≅ ρ. (d) If ρ|_{Γ′} is reducible for an open normal subgroup Γ′ with Γ/Γ′ abelian and ρ is irreducible, then ρ(Γ′) is diagonalisable (char k ∤ |ρ(Γ′)|) and either π(ρ(Γ′)) = 1 (π(ρ(Γ)) cyclic, impossible for irreducible ρ) or ρ is induced from the stabiliser of one eigenline of ρ(Γ′), an index-2 subgroup containing Γ′. (e) In characteristic 2, an irreducible ρ with dihedral projective image has n odd ≥ 3, and det ρ has odd order on ρ(Δ).
hypotheses: k algebraically closed; when k = ℚ̄_ℓ or ℂ the dihedral image is finite by hypothesis
Δ open of index 2; χ continuous for the topology in which ρ is continuous
(c) needs char k ≠ 2 (ε_Δ is trivial modulo 2)
proofSteps: (2) ⇒ (1): in a basis {e, σe} of Ind χ, ρ(δ) = diag(χ(δ), χ^σ(δ)) and ρ(σ) is antidiagonal. Since χ ≠ χ^σ the only Δ-stable lines are the two eigenlines, swapped by σ, so ρ is irreducible (characteristic-free; in characteristic 0 this is also tauceti:TauCeti.simple_indFDRep_ofLinearCharacter_iff). The projective image of Δ is the cyclic group generated by the values of χ/χ^σ, order n ≥ 2 prime to char k; an antidiagonal element is an involution in PGL_2 inverting it, so the image is dihedral of order 2n.

(1) ⇒ (2): let C ⊂ π(ρ(Γ)) be a cyclic subgroup of index 2 and Δ its preimage, open of index 2. ρ(Δ) is a central extension of a cyclic group, hence abelian, and has a common eigenvector over k (tauceti:TauCeti.exists_unitHom_jointEigenvector_of_pairwise_commute_of_isAlgClosed) with character χ. Frobenius reciprocity (R01.1/continuous-induction) gives a nonzero Γ-map ρ → Ind χ, an isomorphism since ρ is irreducible and both have dimension 2; χ = χ^σ would make Ind χ ≅ χ̃ ⊗ k[Γ/Δ] reducible, χ̃ an extension of χ (which exists as H²(ℤ/2, k^×) = k^×/k^{×2} = 1).

(b) The cyclic subgroup of order n ≥ 3 is characteristic in the dihedral group; the Klein group has three subgroups of order 2. The trace of an antidiagonal matrix is 0. The determinant formula is R01.1/determinant-of-induced-representation with rank 1.

(c) Ind χ ⊗ ε_Δ ≅ Ind(χ ⊗ ε_Δ|_Δ) = Ind χ; conversely an isomorphism A : ρ ≅ ρ ⊗ ε_Δ has A² scalar by Schur, A non-scalar (ε_Δ ≠ 1 and char ≠ 2), and its two eigenspaces are Δ-stable lines, so ρ|_Δ is reducible and (1) ⇒ (2) applies with this Δ.

(d) By R01.4/p-subgroups-and-borel-subgroups a reducible normal ρ(Γ′) with char k | |ρ(Γ′)| has a normal unipotent subgroup whose line is Γ-stable; so ρ(Γ′) is diagonalisable (Clifford: tauceti:TauCeti.Representation.isSemisimpleRepresentation_comp_subtype) and Γ permutes its isotypic lines.
(e) In characteristic 2 the image of Δ is diagonalisable, so its projective image has odd order n; n = 2 is excluded since the Klein group would be a 2-group fixing a line.
acceptance: Instance (Swinnerton-Dyer's mod-23 representation): for L the splitting field of x³ − x − 1 (Galois group S_3, quadratic subfield ℚ(√−23)), the standard two-dimensional representation of S_3 over F̄_23 composed with G_ℚ → S_3 is Ind_{G_{ℚ(√−23)}}^{G_ℚ} χ with χ of order 3; projective image S_3, dihedral of order 6.

Klein case: for a biquadratic field ℚ(√a, √b), the representation of Gal ≅ (ℤ/2)² lifted to Q_8 ⊂ SL_2(ℂ) is irreducible with projective image V_4 and is induced from each of the three quadratic subfields.
Characteristic-2 instance: E[2] for E : y² = x³ − 2 is Ind from ℚ(√−3) of a character of order 3 (n = 3 odd).

nodes.title: Bad dihedral representations
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and p* := (−1)^{(p−1)/2} p. For a number field F let K_F := F(ζ_p) and let F′ ⊂ K_F be the fixed field of the subgroup of squares of the cyclic group Gal(K_F/F) (so F′ = F if [K_F : F] is odd, and F′ is the quadratic subextension of K_F/F otherwise). For F = ℚ, F′ = ℚ(√p*), the quadratic subfield of ℚ(ζ_p), equal to ℚ(g) for the quadratic Gauss sum g with g² = p* (mathlib:gaussSum_sq). Let k be a finite field of characteristic p (or k = F̄_p) and ρ̄ : G_F → GL_2(k) continuous. ρ̄ is bad dihedral if ρ̄ is absolutely irreducible and ρ̄|_{G_{F′}} is not absolutely irreducible. For F = ℚ this is Dieulefait–Pacetti Definition 1.12: ρ̄ irreducible (over F̄_p) and ρ̄|_{G_{ℚ(√p*)}} reducible. Equivalently (R01.4/bad-dihedral-representations-and-the-oddness-criterion) ρ̄ is absolutely irreducible and ρ̄|_{G_{F(ζ_p)}} is not; ‘not bad dihedral and absolutely irreducible’ is Wiles's condition ‘ρ̄|_{G_{ℚ(√p*)}} absolutely irreducible’.
hypotheses: p odd
coefficients finite of characteristic p or F̄_p; ‘reducible’ means not absolutely irreducible
F′ is defined by the squares of Gal(F(ζ_p)/F), not by adjoining √p* (for F ∋ √p*, F′ = F(ζ_p)^{Gal²} is different)
proofSteps: Gal(ℚ(ζ_p)/ℚ) ≅ (ℤ/p)^× (mathlib:IsCyclotomicExtension.autEquivPow) is cyclic of even order p − 1, its squares form the unique index-2 subgroup, and its fixed field is ℚ(g) with g² = χ(−1)p = p* for the Legendre character χ (mathlib:gaussSum_sq).
Absolute irreducibility is invariant under extension of k (R01.1/absolutely-irreducible), so the definition does not depend on k.
acceptance: Instance: the mod-23 representation attached to x³ − x − 1 (standard representation of S_3 over F_23 through G_ℚ → Gal(L/ℚ)) is absolutely irreducible and odd, and its restriction to G_{ℚ(√−23)} has image of order 3 with eigenvalues primitive cube roots of unity not in F_23: irreducible over F_23 but not absolutely irreducible. So it is bad dihedral (p = 23, p* = −23).
If p ≥ 5 and ρ̄(G_ℚ) ⊇ SL_2(F_p) then ρ̄ is not bad dihedral (the image of G_{ℚ(√p*)} has index ≤ 2 and contains SL_2(F_p)).

nodes.title: The quadratic–cyclotomic irreducibility criterion and projective inertia of bad dihedral representations
nodes.statement: (a) [cyclic restriction criterion] Let L/F be a finite cyclic Galois extension of fields, F′ ⊂ L the fixed field of the subgroup of squares of Gal(L/F), k an algebraically closed field and ρ : G_F → GL_2(k) a homomorphism with open kernel. Then ρ|_{G_{F′}} is irreducible iff ρ|_{G_L} is irreducible. (b) [Dieulefait–Pacetti Lemma 1.13, strengthened] Let F be a number field, p an odd prime, F′ as in R01.4/bad-dihedral-representation, m ≥ 1 and ρ̄ : G_F → GL_2(k) continuous with k finite of characteristic p. The following are equivalent: (1) ρ̄|_{G_{F′}} absolutely irreducible; (2) ρ̄|_{G_{F(ζ_p)}} absolutely irreducible; (3) ρ̄|_{G_{F(ζ_{p^m})}} absolutely irreducible. No oddness hypothesis is needed (the source assumes ρ̄ odd and F = ℚ). (c) If ρ̄ is bad dihedral then ρ̄ ⊗ F̄_p ≅ Ind_{G_{F′}}^{G_F} χ with χ ≠ χ^σ, the projective image is dihedral of order 2n with p ∤ n, and |ρ̄(G_F)| is prime to p. (d) [Dieulefait–Pacetti Lemma 1.14, inertia part] If F = ℚ and ρ̄ is bad dihedral, then the projective image of ρ̄(I_p) has order ≤ 2. Writing (ρ̄|_{I_p}) ⊗ F̄_p ≅ ψ_1 ⊕ ψ_2 (tame characters, R01.2/tame-semisimple-residual-local-representations), ψ_1/ψ_2 has order ≤ 2: in niveau 1, ψ_1/ψ_2 = ω^a with (p − 1) | 2a; in niveau 2, ψ_1 = ω_2^b, ψ_2 = ω_2^{pb} with (p + 1) | 2b. The translation into Serre weights (p = 2k(ρ̄) − 1 in niveau 1, p = 2k(ρ̄) − 3 in niveau 2, after normalising 2 ≤ k(ρ̄) ≤ p + 1) belongs to AlgebraicModularFormsAndSerreWeights:R15.4 and is not stated here.
hypotheses: (a) is characteristic-free; k algebraically closed
(b)–(d): p odd
(d) uses that ℚ(√p*) is ramified at p and unramified elsewhere; it is stated over ℚ as in the source
proofSteps: (a) ⇐ is clear. ⇒: suppose ρ|_{G_{F′}} irreducible and ρ|_{G_L} reducible. If char k | |ρ(G_L)|, the normal unipotent subgroup O_p(ρ(G_L)) fixes a unique line, which ρ(G_{F′}) stabilises (R01.4/p-subgroups-and-borel-subgroups): contradiction. So ρ(G_L) ≅ ψ_1 ⊕ ψ_2 is diagonalisable. If ψ_1 = ψ_2, ρ(G_L) is scalar, π(ρ(G_{F′})) is cyclic, ρ(G_{F′}) abelian and reducible: contradiction. If ψ_1 ≠ ψ_2, G_F (which normalises G_L) permutes the two eigenlines through G_F/G_L = Gal(L/F) → S_2; every element of Gal(L/F′) is a square in the cyclic group Gal(L/F), so acts trivially, and G_{F′} stabilises both lines: contradiction.

(b) Apply (a) to L = F(ζ_p) and L = F(ζ_{p^m}) (cyclic over F since p is odd); [F(ζ_{p^m}) : F(ζ_p)] is a power of p, odd, so both have the same subfield F′. This replaces the case analysis of the source proof (Borel / split Cartan normaliser / A_4, S_4), which is also correct.

(c) By the proof of (a) with L replaced by F′ and F′ by F (G_{F′} is normal of index 2 in G_F): ρ̄(G_{F′}) is diagonalisable with two distinct characters, G_F swaps the eigenlines, and R01.4/dihedral-projective-image-iff-induced gives ρ̄ ≅ Ind χ; the image of G_{F′} is diagonal of order prime to p and has index 2, and p is odd.

(d) Following the source (after Ribet 1997 Prop. 2.2): the image has no element of order p, so ρ̄|_{I_p} is tame, semisimple, with cyclic projective image. If its order were > 2 it would lie in the unique cyclic subgroup of index 2 of the dihedral projective image, whose fixed field is ℚ(√p*) by (c); that field would then be unramified at p, a contradiction. The niveau computations: ω has order p − 1 and ω_2^{b(1−p)} has order (p + 1)/gcd(p + 1, b).
acceptance: Check both niveau cases on explicit representations: x³ − x − 1 at p = 23 is niveau 1 with ψ_1/ψ_2 of order 2 = ω^{11}; a dihedral representation induced from ℚ(√p*) with niveau-2 inertia ω_2^b ⊕ ω_2^{pb}, (p + 1)/2 | b, illustrates the second case.
Check that the oddness hypothesis is not used: the even representation Ind_{ℚ(√5)}^{ℚ} χ (χ ≠ χ^σ of odd order, p = 5) is irreducible and reducible on both G_{ℚ(√5)} and G_{ℚ(ζ_5)}, as (b) predicts.
Check that at p = 2 the oddness argument of R01.4/odd-irreducible-implies-absolutely-irreducible fails by the F_2-irreducible representation of image order 3 that splits over F_4.

nodes.title: The image of a restriction and linear disjointness
nodes.statement: Let F be a field, ρ : G_F → GL_n(A) continuous with A discrete (finite image), K = F̄^{ker ρ} its kernel field, so that ρ induces an isomorphism Gal(K/F) ≅ ρ(G_F). Let F′/F be a finite separable extension inside F̄. Then: (a) ρ(G_{F′}) is the image of Gal(K/K ∩ F′) ⊂ Gal(K/F) under this isomorphism; (b) if F′ is linearly disjoint from K over F (equivalently K ∩ F′ = F, as K/F is Galois; equivalently [KF′ : F′] = [K : F]), then ρ(G_{F′}) = ρ(G_F); (c) the same holds for the projective image with K replaced by the projective kernel field M = F̄^{ker π∘ρ} ⊂ K, so linear disjointness from M suffices for the projective image; (d) if F′/F is Galois and linearly disjoint from K(μ_p) (resp. from M(μ_p)), then ρ(G_{F′(ζ_p)}) = ρ(G_{F(ζ_p)}) (resp. for projective images); (e) if H ⊂ ρ(G_F) is a perfect subgroup and F′/F is a soluble tower (each step Galois with solvable group), then H ⊂ ρ(G_{F′}); (f) absolute irreducibility, Dickson type and the non-bad-dihedral condition of ρ depend only on the image and so pass to ρ|_{G_{F′}} in cases (b)–(d).
hypotheses: ρ continuous with discrete coefficients (finite image); for ℓ-adic ρ apply the lemma to each finite quotient
linear disjointness of F′ and K over F means K ⊗_F F′ is a field, equivalently [KF′ : F′] = [K : F] since K/F is Galois
proofSteps: Galois theory for the finite Galois extension K/F: restriction G_{F′} → Gal(K/F) has image Gal(K/K ∩ F′) because K/F is Galois (mathlib:IsGalois.intermediateFieldEquivSubgroup); the image is everything iff K ∩ F′ = F iff [KF′ : F′] = [K : F].
(d) The compositum F′(ζ_p) is linearly disjoint from K(ζ_p) over F(ζ_p) when F′ is Galois over F and linearly disjoint from K(ζ_p); apply (b) over F(ζ_p).

(e) For each Galois step F_i ⊂ F_{i+1} with solvable group, ρ(G_{F_{i+1}}) is normal in ρ(G_{F_i}) with solvable quotient, so H ∩ ρ(G_{F_{i+1}}) is normal in H with solvable quotient; H perfect has no nontrivial solvable quotient (mathlib:Group.IsPerfect.not_isSolvable), so H ⊂ ρ(G_{F_{i+1}}).
(f) follows from (b)–(d) as these properties are properties of the subgroup ρ(G_{F′}) ⊂ GL_n.
acceptance: Instance: F = ℚ, ρ̄ = ρ̄_{E,p} surjective onto GL_2(F_p), F′ = ℚ(√d) with d not a square times ±p: ℚ(E[p]) ∩ F′ = ℚ when √d ∉ ℚ(E[p]); the image over F′ is again GL_2(F_p).
Non-example: F′ = ℚ(√p*) ⊂ ℚ(ζ_p) ⊂ ℚ(E[p]) is never linearly disjoint, and ρ̄(G_{F′}) = {g : det g a square} has index 2.

nodes.title: Normal subgroups, quotients and automorphisms of SL_2, PSL_2, PGL_2 over finite fields
nodes.statement: Let k = F_q be a finite field of characteristic p. (a) If q ≥ 4: SL_2(k) is perfect, PSL_2(k) is simple, and every normal subgroup of GL_2(k) either contains SL_2(k) or is central (contained in k^×). The only normal subgroups of SL_2(k) are 1, {±1} ∩ SL_2(k), SL_2(k); hence its only nontrivial quotients are PSL_2(k) and SL_2(k). For q odd the only nontrivial proper normal subgroup of PGL_2(k) is PSL_2(k), of index 2; for q even PGL_2(k) = PSL_2(k) ≅ SL_2(k). Abelianisations: GL_2(k)^{ab} ≅ k^× via det (q ≥ 3), PGL_2(k)^{ab} ≅ k^×/k^{×2}. (b) Small fields: GL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3 has normal subgroup A_3 ≅ ℤ/3 (not central, not containing SL_2(F_2) = GL_2(F_2)); GL_2(F_3) has normal subgroups 1, {±1}, Q_8, SL_2(F_3), GL_2(F_3); PGL_2(F_3) ≅ S_4, PSL_2(F_3) ≅ A_4. In particular ‘central or ⊇ SL_2’ fails for q ≤ 3. (c) Automorphisms (Schreier–van der Waerden, Dieudonné): for q ≥ 4, Aut(PSL_2(F_q)) = Aut(PGL_2(F_q)) = PΓL_2(F_q) = PGL_2(F_q) ⋊ Gal(F_q/F_p), acting by conjugation and by the Frobenius on entries; for q = p ≥ 5 every automorphism of PGL_2(F_p) is inner. Consequently every automorphism of PSL_2(F_q) maps the class of an element with eigenvalue ratio α to one with ratio Frob^i(α), so eigenvalues in F_p are preserved up to scalar. (d) Products: if S is non-abelian simple, a subgroup of S^r projecting onto each factor is isomorphic to S^s, s ≤ r, cut out by diagonal identifications through automorphisms (Goursat), and Aut(S^r) = Aut(S)^r ⋊ S_r. (e) For two continuous ρ̄_1, ρ̄_2 : G_F → GL_2(k̄) whose projective images are PSL_2(F_q) or PGL_2(F_q), q ≥ 4, the projective kernel fields M_1, M_2 satisfy M_1 ∩ M_2 ∈ {F, a quadratic extension, M_1 = M_2}; if M_1 = M_2 then the projective representations are conjugate up to a Frobenius automorphism of F_q.
hypotheses: (c) is quoted from the literature (Dieudonné 1951/1963, Steinberg), not reproved; its proof is sketched
proofSteps: (a) Perfectness and simplicity are in Mathlib (mathlib:Matrix.SL2.commutator_eq_top, mathlib:Matrix.ProjectiveSpecialLinearGroup.rank_two_simple). For N ⊴ GL_2(k): N ∩ SL_2 maps to a normal subgroup of PSL_2, trivial or all. If all, (N ∩ SL_2)·Z = SL_2 and perfectness gives SL_2 = [SL_2, SL_2] ⊂ N. If trivial, [N, GL_2] ⊂ N ∩ SL_2 ⊂ {±1}; for g ∈ N, h ↦ [g, h] is a homomorphism SL_2 → {±1}, trivial by perfectness, so g centralises SL_2(k), whose k-span is M_2(k), so g is scalar (mathlib:Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup.center_eq_range_scalar).

Quotients of SL_2: a normal subgroup not containing SL_2 is central, i.e. inside {±1}. PGL_2(k)/PSL_2(k) ≅ k^×/k^{×2} via det; a normal subgroup of PGL_2 meets PSL_2 in 1 or PSL_2; in the first case it centralises PSL_2, hence is trivial.
(b) by direct computation in groups of order 6 and 48.

(c) An automorphism permutes the q + 1 Sylow p-subgroups (unipotent radicals of Borels, R01.4/p-subgroups-and-borel-subgroups), i.e. acts on P¹(F_q), normalising the image of PSL_2(F_q) in Sym(P¹(F_q)); that normaliser is PΓL_2(F_q) (Dieudonné, La géométrie des groupes classiques, Ch. IV §6; Steinberg's theorem on automorphisms of Chevalley groups for the general case, as cited by Boxer–Calegari–Gee–Newton–Thorne Lemma 5.2.3). For q = p, Gal(F_p/F_p) = 1.
(d) Goursat's lemma (mathlib:Subgroup.goursat) and simplicity by induction on r; minimal normal subgroups of S^r are the factors.

(e) Gal(M_1 ∩ M_2/F) is a common quotient of the two projective images; by (a) their nontrivial quotients are ℤ/2 and the group itself. If M_1 = M_2, the two projective representations differ by an automorphism of the image, which is given by (c).
acceptance: PGL_2(F_5) ≅ S_5 and PSL_2(F_5) ≅ A_5: Aut(A_5) = S_5 = PGL_2(F_5), all automorphisms of PGL_2(F_5) inner, consistent with (c) for q = p = 5.
PSL_2(F_9) ≅ A_6: Aut(A_6) has order 1440 = 2·|PGL_2(F_9)| = |PΓL_2(F_9)|, so the Frobenius of F_9 gives automorphisms not induced by PGL_2(F_9); ‘every automorphism is inner’ needs q = p.
For q = 3 the claim of Allen et al. Lemma 7.1.8(2) proof that normal subgroups of GL_2(F_l) are central or contain SL_2 fails (Q_8 ⊴ GL_2(F_3)); see PAPER-ALLEN-ETAL-23/E100.

nodes.title: Residual images under restriction to cyclotomic fields
nodes.statement: Let F be a number field, p a prime, k a finite field of characteristic p and ρ̄ : G_F → GL_2(k) continuous; write G = ρ̄(G_F), H = ρ̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}) ⊴ G with G/H a quotient of Gal(F(ζ_p)/F) ⊂ (ℤ/p)^× (cyclic). (a) [cyclic restriction] For p odd and m ≥ 1, ρ̄|_{G_{F(ζ_{p^m})}} is absolutely irreducible iff ρ̄|_{G_{F(ζ_p)}} is iff ρ̄|_{G_{F′}} is (R01.4/bad-dihedral-representations-and-the-oddness-criterion). (b) [Caraiani–Newton Lemma 7.1.1(1)] If ρ̄ is irreducible and ρ̄|_{G_{F(ζ_p)}} is absolutely reducible, then G lies in the normaliser of a Cartan subgroup of GL_2(k) (in the Cartan itself if ρ̄ is not absolutely irreducible). (c) [CN 7.1.1(2),(3)] If moreover k = F_p and det ρ̄ = χ̄_p: for p = 3, G is conjugate to C_s^+(3) or to a subgroup of C_ns(3); for p = 5 and [F(ζ_5) : F] = 4, G is conjugate to a subgroup of C_ns^+(5). (d) [big-image bookkeeping, BCGNT] If p ≥ 5, SL_2(F_p) ⊂ G ⊂ GL_2(F_p) and det ρ̄ is trivial on G_{F(ζ_p)} (for instance det ρ̄ = χ̄_p^{−m}), then H = SL_2(F_p). More generally if G ⊃ SL_2(F_q), q ≥ 4, then H ⊃ SL_2(F_q), and H's projective image is PSL_2(F_q) or PGL_2(F_q)-type by R01.4/dickson-classification-and-the-dyadic-refinement. (e) [Allen et al. Lemma 7.1.6(1)] If p > 3, F′/F is finite, ρ̄(G_{F̃}) ⊃ SL_2(F_p) for the normal closure F̃ of F, F′ is linearly disjoint from F̄^{ker ρ̄} over F and p is unramified in F′/ℚ, then ζ_p ∉ F̄^{ker ad ρ̄}·F′: the projective image PSL_2(k_0) or PGL_2(k_0) has no cyclic quotient of order p − 1 > 2 while Gal(F′(ζ_p)/F′) ≅ (ℤ/p)^×. (f) [Caraiani–Newton Lemma 6.1.4] If ζ_5 ∉ F and the projective image of ρ̄(G_{F(ζ_5)}) is conjugate to PSL_2(F_5), with ρ̄(G_F) ⊂ GL_2(F_5) and det ρ̄ = χ̄_5, then the field cut out by the projective image of ρ̄(G_F) does not contain ζ_5. (g) [Allen et al. Lemma 7.1.8(2), group part] If l ≥ 3 and Δ ⊴ GL_2(F_l) has det(Δ) = F_l^×, then Δ = GL_2(F_l). (h) For p > 2 and ρ̄|_{G_{F(ζ_p)}} absolutely irreducible: no nonzero X ∈ M_2(k) with Tr X = 0 satisfies ρ̄(σ)Xρ̄(σ)⁻¹ = X for all σ ∈ G_F, and none satisfies ρ̄(σ)Xρ̄(σ)⁻¹ = χ̄_p(σ)X for all σ (the invariants H⁰(G_F, ad⁰ρ̄) and H⁰(G_F, ad⁰ρ̄(1)) vanish once G7/adjoint-representations identifies ad⁰ρ̄ with this module).
hypotheses: p prime; in (a), (h) p odd; in (d), (e) p ≥ 5 (perfectness of SL_2(F_p))
(e) requires p unramified in F′, so that [F′(ζ_p) : F′] = p − 1
(g) needs l ≥ 3: for l = 2, A_3 ⊴ GL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3 has det(A_3) = F_2^× = {1} but A_3 ≠ GL_2(F_2); Allen et al. print Lemma 7.1.8(2) without l > 2 (PAPER-ALLEN-ETAL-23/E100)
proofSteps: (a) is R01.4/bad-dihedral-representations-and-the-oddness-criterion (b).

(b) H is absolutely reducible and normal in G; by R01.4/dihedral-projective-image-iff-induced (d) and R01.4/p-subgroups-and-borel-subgroups, H is diagonalisable over k̄ with eigenlines {D_1, D_2}, a Frobenius-stable pair; G permutes it, so G lies in the normaliser of the split (D_i rational) or non-split (D_i conjugate over F_{q²}) Cartan attached to it; if H is scalar, π(G) is cyclic, G abelian, contained in a Cartan. CN prove (1) with [FLHS15, Lemma 2.2].
(c) Case analysis of irreducible subgroups of N(C) ⊂ GL_2(F_3), GL_2(F_5) with surjective determinant, following CN's proof via [FLHS15, Prop. 4.1(b)].
(d) det is trivial on G_{F(ζ_p)} so H ⊂ SL_2(F_p) ∩ G; G/H is abelian, so H ⊃ [G, G] ⊃ [SL_2(F_p), SL_2(F_p)] = SL_2(F_p) by mathlib:Matrix.SL2.commutator_eq_top.

(e) As in Allen et al.: reduce to m = 1; by R01.4/image-of-restriction-to-a-subfield the projective image over F′ equals that over F, which is PSL_2(k_0) or PGL_2(k_0) (R01.4/dickson-classification-and-the-dyadic-refinement (c)) with abelianisation of order ≤ 2 (R01.4/normal-subgroups-and-automorphisms-of-psl2-pgl2); if ζ_p were in the compositum, (ℤ/p)^× of order p − 1 > 2 would be a quotient.
(f) CN: ρ̄(G_{F(ζ_5)}) ⊂ SL_2(F_5) surjects onto PSL_2(F_5), so equals SL_2(F_5); compare [G : H] with [F(ζ_5) : F] according as det ρ̄ has order 2 or 4.

(g) By R01.4/normal-subgroups-and-automorphisms-of-psl2-pgl2 (a) for l ≥ 5, Δ is central (det(Δ) ⊂ squares, not all of F_l^×) or contains SL_2(F_l); for l = 3 every proper normal subgroup of GL_2(F_3) lies in SL_2(F_3) (list (b)).

(h) An X of the first kind commutes with the absolutely irreducible ρ̄(G_{F(ζ_p)}), so is scalar by Schur, hence 0 as Tr X = 2x and p ≠ 2; an X of the second kind is invariant under G_{F(ζ_p)} (χ̄_p trivial there), hence scalar, and Tr X = 0 forces X = 0.
acceptance: Instance: for E/ℚ with surjective mod-p image, p ≥ 5, the image of G_{ℚ(ζ_p)} on E[p] is SL_2(F_p) by (d).
Instance (CN): for p = 5 and [F(ζ_5) : F] = 4, an irreducible ρ̄ with cyclotomically reducible restriction has image in C_ns^+(5).
Non-example for (g) at l = 3 in the source's form: Q_8 ⊴ GL_2(F_3) is neither central nor ⊇ SL_2(F_3).

nodes.title: Large residual image: persistence under small index and soluble base change, and a tame-inertia criterion
nodes.statement: Let p ≥ 5 and G ⊂ GL_2(F̄_p) a finite subgroup containing a conjugate of SL_2(F_{p^a}) with p^a ≥ 5. (a) [Newton–Thorne Lemma 2.3(3), group part] If a ≥ 2, every subgroup H ⊂ G of index [G : H] < 2p contains gSL_2(F_{p^a})g⁻¹, the same conjugate that G contains. The bound a ≥ 2 is needed (Newton–Thorne assume a ≥ a_0(p) ≥ 3): for a = 1 the Borel subgroup of SL_2(F_p) has index p + 1 < 2p. (b) [perfect subgroups] If H ⊂ ρ̄(G_F) is perfect (e.g. a conjugate of SL_2(F_{p^a}), p^a ≥ 4), it remains in the image after restriction to any soluble tower F′/F (R01.4/image-of-restriction-to-a-subfield (e)); in particular ‘ρ̄(G_F) contains a conjugate of SL_2(F_{p^a})’ survives soluble base change. (c) [tame-inertia criterion, after Boxer–Calegari–Gee Theorem 3.1] Let ρ̄ : G_ℚ → GL_2(F̄_p) be continuous, unramified outside p, with ρ̄|_{G_{ℚ_p}} absolutely irreducible and ρ̄|_{I_p} ≅ ω_2^{a} ⊕ ω_2^{pa} for an integer a with gcd(a, p + 1) = 1. Then ρ̄(G_ℚ) contains a conjugate of SL_2(F_p). Statements that need automorphic input (Newton–Thorne Proposition 5.4 and Theorem 5.9, large image from tamely dihedral local components) are not stated here; their group-theoretic step is R01.4/dickson-classification-and-the-dyadic-refinement (e).
hypotheses: p ≥ 5 in (a), (c)
(c) uses fundamental characters ω_2 of niveau 2 (R01.2/tame-inertia-and-fundamental-characters)
proofSteps: (a) Put S = gSL_2(F_{p^a})g⁻¹ ⊂ G and q = p^a. Then [S : H ∩ S] ≤ [G : H] < 2p. By Galois's theorem (Dickson §262) a proper subgroup of PSL_2(F_q) has index ≥ q + 1 unless q ∈ {2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11}; a proper subgroup of SL_2(F_q) maps to a proper subgroup of PSL_2(F_q) (a subgroup surjecting onto PSL_2 is all of the perfect group SL_2, mathlib:Matrix.SL2.commutator_eq_top), so it has index ≥ q + 1 as well. For a ≥ 2, q ≥ 25 and q + 1 > 2p, so H ∩ S = S. Newton–Thorne quote Lemma 2.3 from Thorne 2024 Lemma 7.3; the adequacy parts (1)–(2) belong to ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations:G7.
(b) Group.IsPerfect has no nontrivial solvable quotient; apply R01.4/image-of-restriction-to-a-subfield (e).

(c) The projective image of I_p is generated by ω_2^{a(1−p)}, of order (p + 1)/gcd(p + 1, a) = p + 1 > 5, so π(ρ̄(G_ℚ)) is not A_4, S_4, A_5 (R01.4/dickson-classification-and-the-dyadic-refinement (e)); it is not in a Borel since ρ̄|_{G_{ℚ_p}} is absolutely irreducible. If it were dihedral, ρ̄ would be induced from the quadratic field cut out by the rotation subgroup (R01.4/dihedral-projective-image-iff-induced), unramified outside p, hence ℚ(√p*); then ρ̄|_{G_{ℚ_p}} is induced from ℚ_p(√p*) and hence ≅ ρ̄|_{G_{ℚ_p}} ⊗ η with η the quadratic character of ℚ_p(√p*)/ℚ_p, η|_{I_p} = ω^{(p−1)/2} = ω_2^{(p²−1)/2}. Comparing {ω_2^{a}, ω_2^{pa}} with {ω_2^{a+(p²−1)/2}, ω_2^{pa+(p²−1)/2}}: the first cannot match itself (ω_2 has order p² − 1), so ω_2^{a+(p²−1)/2} = ω_2^{pa}, i.e. (p − 1)a ≡ (p² − 1)/2 mod p² − 1, i.e. a ≡ (p + 1)/2 mod p + 1, and then gcd(a, p + 1) = (p + 1)/2 > 1, a contradiction (Boxer–Calegari–Gee write this as k ≡ (p + 3)/2 mod p + 1 for a = 1 − k, up to their sign convention, sourceIssue PAPER-BOXER-CALEGARI-GEE-25/E9). The remaining case PSL_2/PGL_2(F_{p^s}) gives SL_2(F_{p^s}) ⊂ ρ̄(G_ℚ) by (c) of the Dickson node.
acceptance: Instance (BCG25): for the weight-26 form ΔE_4²E_6 at p = 107, non-ordinary with gcd(k − 1, p + 1) = 1, the residual image contains SL_2(F_107); its determinant ε̄^{−25} is surjective, so the image is GL_2(F_107) (Swinnerton-Dyer's computation, maintainer item PAPER-BOXER-CALEGARI-GEE-25/sd73-image; the modular-form input is not planned here).
Sharpness for a = 1: in SL_2(F_5) ≅ 2.A_5 the subgroup SL_2(F_3) ≅ 2.A_4 has index 5 < 10 and the Borel has index 6 < 10; neither contains SL_2(F_5).

nodes.title: Characteristic two: non-solvable residual images and the module M_2(F)
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field of characteristic 2, F_0 ⊂ F a subfield with |F_0| = 2^r, r ≥ 2, and G_0 = SL_2(F_0) ≅ PGL_2(F_0) acting on Ad := M_2(F) by conjugation (through SL_2(F_0) ⊂ GL_2(F)); Z := F·1 ⊂ Ad^0 := {X : Tr X = 0} ⊂ Ad (Z ⊂ Ad^0 since Tr 1 = 2 = 0). Let ρ̄ : G_K → GL_2(F) be continuous and absolutely irreducible with non-solvable image, K a number field. (a) [projective image] π(ρ̄(G_K)) is conjugate to PGL_2(F_0) = PSL_2(F_0) ≅ SL_2(F_0) for some F_0 ⊂ F with |F_0| ≥ 4 (R01.4/dickson-classification-and-the-dyadic-refinement (d)). (b) [Khare–Wintenberger II Lemma 4.3(2)(ii)] H⁰(G_0, Ad) = H⁰(G_0, Ad^0) = Z is one-dimensional, and H⁰(G_0, Ad/Z) = H⁰(G_0, (Ad^0)^*) = 0, where (Ad^0)^* ≅ Ad/Z through the trace pairing. (c) [KW II Lemma 4.3(5)(i), Dickinson Lemma 42] H¹(SL_2(F_0), M_2(F)) = 0. (d) [KW II Lemma 4.3(5)(ii)] The only G_0-submodules of Ad are 0, Z, Ad^0, Ad; the only nonzero irreducible submodule is Z. (e) Every one-dimensional F[G_0]-module is trivial (G_0 perfect), and Ad^0/Z is the Frobenius-twisted natural representation, irreducible of dimension 2.
hypotheses: characteristic 2 and |F_0| ≥ 4 (for F_0 = F_2, SL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3 is solvable and (b)–(d) fail)
(c) is quoted from Dickinson (Duke 2001) through KW II; Dickinson's paper was not read (see gaps)
proofSteps: (b) As in KW II: an element of Ad^G0 commutes with the absolutely irreducible SL_2(F_0), so is scalar (Schur); Ad^0 ∋ 1. For Ad/Z: if l ∈ Ad maps to a nonzero invariant of Ad/Z, take g ∈ G_0 semisimple non-scalar with eigenlines D_1, D_2; Ad(g) acts unipotently on the plane P = ⟨1, l⟩ and 1 is not an eigenvalue on Ad/P, so P is the diagonal subalgebra for D_1 ⊕ D_2; P is G_0-stable, so G_0 stabilises {D_1, D_2} and would be solvable, a contradiction. The trace pairing identifies (Ad^0)^* with Ad/Z.

(c) Dickinson Lemma 42, quoted by KW II; equivalently Ext¹_{F[SL_2(F_0)]}(V, V) = 0 for the natural module V = F², since H¹(G, Hom(V, V)) = Ext¹(V, V). The composition factors of Ad are Z ≅ F, Ad^0/Z ≅ V^{(2)} (torus weights λ^{±2}) and Ad/Ad^0 ≅ F (trace), and H¹(SL_2(F_0), F) = 0 (perfect); the vanishing of H¹(G_0, Ad) is not a formal consequence of these factors and is Dickinson's computation.

(d) KW II: 1-dimensional submodules are trivial, hence inside H⁰ = Z; a 2-dimensional submodule of Ad^0 would give a trivial quotient Ad^0 → F, a nonzero element of H⁰((Ad^0)^*), contradicting (b); a 2-dimensional V ⊂ Ad meets Ad^0 in Z, and V/Z ⊂ Ad/Z would be a trivial line, contradicting H⁰(Ad/Z) = 0; a 3-dimensional V ≠ Ad^0 meets Ad^0 in dimension ≥ 2, so contains Ad^0 and equals it.
(e) mathlib:Matrix.SL2.commutator_eq_top (|F_0| ≥ 4 provides a with a ≠ 0, a² ≠ 1).
acceptance: Instance: F_0 = F = F_4, G_0 = SL_2(F_4) ≅ A_5 acting on M_2(F_4): Z ⊂ Ad^0 ⊂ Ad with Ad^0/Z ≅ V^{(2)} of dimension 2, irreducible.
Degenerate failure: for F_0 = F_2, SL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3 has abelianisation ℤ/2, so H¹(S_3, F_2) ≠ 0 and S_3 is solvable; r ≥ 2 is necessary for (a), (e) and for H¹(G_0, Z) = 0.
Odd p contrast: for p odd, Ad = Z ⊕ Ad^0 and H¹(SL_2(F_p), ad^0) is owned by ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations:G7 (G7/h1-of-sl2-with-adjoint-coefficients).

nodes.title: Density of Frobenius elements
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, G_K = Field.absoluteGaloisGroup K with its Krull topology, and Σ a set of finite places of K of Dirichlet density 1 (HasDirichletDensity Σ 1; every cofinite set qualifies). Call σ ∈ G_K a Σ-Frobenius if σ is an arithmetic Frobenius lift at some place w of K̄ above some v ∈ Σ, i.e. σ ∈ D_w and σ(x) ≡ x^{q_v} modulo the maximal ideal of w for all integral x (R01.2/decomposition-group-at-a-place). Then: (a) the set Frob(Σ) of Σ-Frobenius elements is dense in G_K; more precisely, for every open normal subgroup U ⊴ G_K and every g ∈ G_K, the set of v ∈ Σ unramified in L = K̄^U for which some w | v has every Frobenius lift at w in gU has Dirichlet density at least 1/[G_K : U] (exactly #C/[G_K:U] for the conjugacy class C of gU in Gal(L/K)). (b) If φ : G_K → H is a continuous homomorphism to a Hausdorff topological group with φ(I_w) = 1 for every w above every v ∈ Σ, then φ(Frob_w) depends only on w, the set {φ(Frob_w) : w | v, v ∈ Σ} is dense in the compact subgroup φ(G_K), and every closed subset of H that contains φ(Frob_w) for all w above v ∈ Σ contains φ(G_K). (c) In particular, for any finite set S of finite places and continuous ρ : G_K → GL_n(A) unramified outside S (A a Hausdorff topological ring), the elements ρ(Frob_w), w | v, v ∉ S ∪ T, are dense in ρ(G_K) for every finite T, and any continuous function on ρ(G_K) (e.g. γ ↦ det(X − γ) coefficientwise) vanishing at all of them vanishes on ρ(G_K).
hypotheses: K a number field; finite places only (real places may ramify; no condition at infinity).
Σ has Dirichlet density 1 in the sense of ArithmeticDirichletSeries layer 7 (ratio to the all-prime sum); a set of natural density 1 also has Dirichlet density 1.
In (b) and (c) the target is Hausdorff and φ (resp. ρ) kills inertia at every place of Σ (resp. outside S), so that φ(Frob_w) is independent of the Frobenius lift.
Arithmetic Frobenius (x ↦ x^{q_v}); the statement is unchanged for geometric Frobenius because inversion is a homeomorphism preserving conjugacy classes.
proofSteps: Reduce (a) to a finite quotient: a basic open set of G_K is a coset gU with U open normal; L = K̄^U is finite Galois over K (Krull topology) and only finitely many v ramify in L (NumberFieldArithmetic layer 6 / tauceti:NumberField.Chebotarev.finite_compl_iUnion_frobeniusPrimeSet).

Apply the Chebotarev density theorem of tauceti:TauCetiRoadmap/Chebotarev layer 10 (hasDirichletDensity_frobeniusPrimeSet) to L/K and the class C of g|_L: frobeniusPrimeSet K L C has Dirichlet density #C/#Gal(L/K) > 0.

Intersect with Σ: the complement of Σ has density 0, so Σ ∩ frobeniusPrimeSet K L C has positive upper density and is in particular nonempty and infinite (density API of ArithmeticDirichletSeries layer 7: a set of positive density is not contained in a density-zero set).

For v in the intersection, tauceti:NumberField.Chebotarev.mem_frobeniusPrimeSet_mk_iff_exists_isArithFrobAt gives a prime Q of O_L above v with g|_L an arithmetic Frobenius at Q (mathlib:IsArithFrobAt); extend Q to a place w of K̄. Any arithmetic Frobenius lift σ at w restricts to the unique Frobenius of the unramified prime Q (Mathlib uniqueness at unramified primes, NumberFieldArithmetic layer 2.2), so σ|_L = g|_L, i.e. σ ∈ gU.

(b): φ(Frob_w) is well defined because two Frobenius lifts at w differ by I_w ⊂ ker φ. For an open V ⊂ H meeting φ(G_K), φ^{-1}(V) is a nonempty open subset of G_K and so contains some gU; (a) gives a Σ-Frobenius in gU, whose image lies in V. φ(G_K) is compact, hence closed in H, which gives the closure statement.

(c) is (b) for φ = ρ restricted to Σ = (all finite places) ∖ (S ∪ T), which has density 1 because finite sets have density 0; the vanishing statement is the closure statement applied to the zero set of a continuous function.
acceptance: DDT Theorem 2.3 is the special case K = ℚ, Σ = all primes outside S, H = Gal(F/ℚ) for F/ℚ Galois unramified outside S: the union of the Frobenius classes is dense.

For K = ℚ and U = G_{ℚ(ζ_5)}, every coset of U contains Frobenius lifts at primes p ≡ a mod 5 for each a ∈ (ℤ/5)^× (arithmetic Frobenius maps to p mod 5, Chebotarev acceptance test 4), and these primes have density 1/4 each.

Non-example: the set of Frobenius lifts at a single fixed place w is the coset Frob_w·I_w, which is not dense in G_ℚ; density needs infinitely many places, and a set Σ of density 1/2 such as the primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 (split completely in ℚ(i)) gives Frobenius lifts lying in the closed subgroup G_{ℚ(i)}, again not dense: density one is used to meet every Chebotarev set.

sources.match: The density of Frobenius classes in the Galois group of an extension unramified outside S (the text layer renders the union symbol and ∉ as shown); here generalised to any number field and any density-one set of places.
The Chebotarev step applied to a finite image (φ rendered as '(p' by the text layer).

nodes.title: Every element of a finite image is a Frobenius at a set of primes of positive density
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, H a finite group with the discrete topology and φ : G_K → H a continuous homomorphism (for instance ρ : G_K → GL_n(k) continuous with k finite, or with finite image in GL_n(ℂ), R01.1/finite-coefficients-and-finite-quotients). Let S be the finite set of finite places at which φ is ramified and T any finite set of finite places. Then for every h ∈ φ(G_K) the set of v ∉ S ∪ T such that h = φ(Frob_w) for some place w | v has Dirichlet density #(conjugacy class of h in φ(G_K))/#φ(G_K) > 0, and in particular is infinite. Consequently every polynomial identity in the entries of φ(Frob_v) (resp. every statement about det(X − ρ(Frob_v))) that holds for all v outside a finite set holds for every element of the image.
hypotheses: H finite discrete, so ker φ is open and L = K̄^{ker φ} is a finite Galois extension with Gal(L/K) ≅ φ(G_K).
Only places v outside the ramification set S of φ (equivalently, unramified in L) are used; T is arbitrary finite.
The class of h is taken in the image φ(G_K), not in H.
proofSteps: φ factors through Gal(L/K) ≅ φ(G_K) with L = K̄^{ker φ} finite Galois (R01.1/finite-coefficients-and-finite-quotients); v is unramified in L iff φ is unramified at v (R01.2/unramified-and-ramification-set).

Apply hasDirichletDensity_frobeniusPrimeSet (Chebotarev layer 10) to the class C of the element of Gal(L/K) corresponding to h; removing the finite set S ∪ T does not change the density (hasDirichletDensity_of_symmDiff_finite, ArithmeticDirichletSeries layer 7).

For v in the set, tauceti:NumberField.Chebotarev.mem_frobeniusPrimeSet_mk_iff_exists_isArithFrobAt gives a prime of L above v at which the chosen representative is an arithmetic Frobenius; extend it to w | v in K̄, so h = φ(Frob_w).
The consequence: the identity holds at h because h is φ(Frob_w) for some v outside the given finite exceptional set.
acceptance: Deligne–Serre 6.12: for the semisimplified reduction φ of a mod-λ eigenform representation, every s ∈ φ(G) is F_p for some p ∤ Nl, so the coefficients of det(1 − sT) lie in k_f (6.12.1).
For φ : G_ℚ → Gal(ℚ(ζ_7)^+/ℚ) ≅ ℤ/3, the nontrivial elements are Frob_p exactly for p ≡ ±2, ±3 mod 7, a set of density 2/3; p = 2 is one of them.

EllipticModularityEffectiveComparisons EC.3: if the mod-2 representation of an elliptic curve over ℚ has image containing an element of order 3, there is a good odd prime q with Frob_q of order 3 on E[2], hence 1 − Frob_q invertible on E[2] and #E(F_q) odd.

sources.match: Exactly this lemma for G = Gal(Q̄/Q) and a finite image; the continuation (garbled in the text layer) states that every element of φ(G) is F_p with p ∤ Nl.
The density #C/#G of each Frobenius class.

nodes.title: Primes with prescribed quadratic residue symbols, possibly coincident quadratic fields
nodes.statement: Let d_1, …, d_r be nonzero integers and ε_1, …, ε_r ∈ {±1}. The following are equivalent: (i) there are infinitely many odd primes p ∤ d_1⋯d_r with legendreSym p d_i = ε_i for all i; (ii) the set of such primes has Dirichlet density 2^{-m} > 0, where 2^m = [ℚ(√d_1, …, √d_r) : ℚ]; (iii) for every subset J ⊆ {1, …, r} with ∏_{i∈J} d_i a square in ℚ, ∏_{i∈J} ε_i = 1. In particular, for two non-squares d_1, d_2 (the fields ℚ(√d_1), ℚ(√d_2) may coincide, i.e. d_1d_2 may be a square) there are infinitely many primes at which both are quadratic nonresidues; for three non-squares with d_1d_2d_3 a square there are none.
hypotheses: d_i ∈ ℤ ∖ {0}; primes p = 2 and p | d_i are excluded.
Legendre symbols, Mathlib legendreSym; arithmetic Frobenius.
proofSteps: Let M = ℚ(√d_1, …, √d_r) ⊂ ℚ̄, a multiquadratic Galois extension; Kummer theory identifies Gal(M/ℚ) with the dual of the subgroup Δ of ℚ^×/ℚ^{×2} generated by the d_i, σ ↦ (d ↦ σ(√d)/√d) (Tau Ceti Multiquadratic layer 0).
For an odd prime p ∤ ∏ d_i, every arithmetic Frobenius σ at a prime above p satisfies σ(√d_i) = legendreSym p d_i · √d_i (tauceti:NumberField.exists_isArithFrobAt_multiquadratic).

Hence the primes in question are those whose Frobenius is the element ε ∈ Gal(M/ℚ) with ε(√d_i) = ε_i√d_i, which exists iff the assignment d_i ↦ ε_i is a well-defined character of Δ, i.e. iff (iii) holds.

If ε exists, Chebotarev layer 10 (Gal(M/ℚ) abelian, so the class is a singleton) gives Dirichlet density 1/#Gal(M/ℚ) = 2^{-m}; R01.5/every-element-of-a-finite-image-is-a-frobenius packages this. If it does not exist, the set is empty.
acceptance: d_1 = 2, d_2 = 8 (coincident fields ℚ(√2)): both are nonresidues exactly at p ≡ ±3 mod 8, density 1/2.
d_1 = 2, d_2 = 3, d_3 = 6: no prime has all three symbols −1, since (2/p)(3/p) = (6/p); condition (iii) fails for J = {1,2,3}.

EllipticModularityEffectiveComparisons EC.3/four-count-square-classes: for C: y² = x(x² + ax + b) with neither b nor a² − 4b a square, there are infinitely many good odd q at which both are nonresidues.
